enchorial: Belonging to, or used in, a country; native; domestic; popular; common; -- said especially of the written characters employed by the common people of ancient Egypt, in distinction from the hieroglyphics. See Demotic.
entitative: Considered as pure entity; abstracted from all circumstances. Ellis. -- En"ti*ta*tive*ly, adv.

enthronize: To place on a throne; hence, to induct into office, as a bishop. There openly enthronized as the very elected king. Knolles.
entoblast: The inner germ layer; endoderm. See Nucleolus.
engregge: To aggravate; to make worse; to lie heavy on. (old) Chaucer.
enteradenography: A treatise upon, or description of, the intestinal glands.
enguard: To surround as with a guard. (old) Shak.
endamageable: Capable of being damaged, or injured; damageable. (old)
enormous: 1. Exceeding the usual rule, norm, or measure; out of due proportion; inordinate; abnormal. "Enormous bliss." Milton. "This enormous state." Shak. "The hoop's enormous size." Jenyns. ens: 1. (Metaph.) Entity, being, or existence; an actually existing being; also, God, as the Being of Beings. 2. (Chem.) Something supposed to condense within itself all the virtues and qualities of a substance from which it is extracted; essence. (old)
enneapetalous: Having nine petals, or flower leaves.
encyclic: Sent to many persons or places; intended for many, or for a whole order of men; general; circular; as, an encyclical letter of a council, of a bishop, or the pope. | An encyclical letter, esp. one from a pope. Shipley.
ensober: To make sober. (old) Sad accidents to ensober his spirits. Jer. Taylor.
engineercorps: (a) In the United States army, the Corps of Engineers, a corps of officers and enlisted men consisting of one band and three battalions of engineers commanded by a brigadier general, whose title is Chief of Engineers.

endocardium: The membrane lining the cavities of the heart.
enrank: To place in ranks or in order. Shak.
enmesh: To catch or entangle in, or as in, meshes. Shak. My doubts enmesh me if I try. Lowell.
enpassant: In passing; in the course of any procedure; -- said specif. (Chess), of the taking of an adverse pawn which makes a first move of two squares by a pawn already so advanced as to threaten the first of these squares. The pawn which takes en passant is advanced to the threatened square.
endosmometer: An instrument for measuring the force or amount of endosmotic action.
enclavement: The state of being an enclave. [Recent]
enounce: 1. To announce; to declare; to state, as a proposition or argument. Sir W. Hamilton. 2. To utter; to articulate. The student should be able to enounce these [sounds] independently. A. M. Bell.
entresol: A low story between two higher ones, usually between the ground floor and the first story; mezzanine. Parker.
enterorrhaphy: The operation of sewing up a rent in the intestinal canal.
enallage: A substitution, as of one part of speech for another, of one gender, number, case, person, tense, mode, or voice, of the same word, for another.

entrail: To interweave; to intertwine. (old) Spenser. | Entanglement; fold. (old) Spenser.
encollar: To furnish or surround with a collar.
enwoman: To endow with the qualities of a woman. Daniel.
encrinoidea: That order of the Crinoidea which includes most of the living and many fossil forms, having jointed arms around the margin of the oral disk; -- also called Brachiata and Articulata. See Illusts. under Comatula and Crinoidea.
enfeoffment: (a) The act of enfeoffing. (b) The instrument or deed by which one is invested with the fee of an estate.

enoptomancy: Divination by the use of a mirror.
enhancer: One who enhances; one who, or that which, raises the amount, price, etc.
endosarc: The semifluid, granular interior of certain unicellular organisms, as the inner layer of sarcode in the amoeba; entoplasm; endoplasta.
enfranchisement: 1. Releasing from slavery or custody. Shak. 2. Admission to the freedom of a corporation or body politic; investiture with the privileges of free citizens. Enfranchisement of copyhold (Eng. Law), the conversion of a copyhold estate into a freehold. Mozley & W.
encephalotomy: The act or art of dissecting the brain.
endless: 1. enigmatize: To make, or talk in, enigmas; to deal in riddles.
encrinal: Relating to encrinites; containing encrinites, as certain kinds of limestone.
ennead: The number nine or a group of nine. The Enneads, the title given to the works of the philosopher Plotinus, published by his pupil Porphyry; -- so called because each of the six books into which it is divided contains nine chapters.
enecate: To kill off; to destroy. (old) Harvey.
entity: A real being, whether in thought (as an ideal conception) or in fact; being; essence; existence. Self-subsisting entities, such as our own personality. Shairp. Fortune is no real entity, . . . but a mere relative signification. Bentley.
enlight: To illumine; to enlighten. Which from the first has shone on ages past, Enlights the present, and shall warm the last. Pope.
entomostracan: Relating to the Entomostraca. -- n. One of the Entomostraca.

enrange: 1. To range in order; to put in rank; to arrange. (old) Spenser. 2. To rove over; to range. (old) Spenser.
ennui: A feeling of weariness and disgust; dullness and languor of spirits, arising from satiety or want of interest; tedium. T. Gray.
entomoid: Resembling an insect. -- n. An object resembling an insect.
endecane: One of the higher hydrocarbons of the paraffin series, C11H24, found as a constituent of petroleum. [Written also hendecane.]
entocuniform: One of the bones of the tarsus. See Cuneiform.
endolymphatic: (a) Pertaining to, or containing, endolymph; as, the endolymphatic duct. (b) Within a lymphatic vessel; endolymphangial.
enucleate: 1. To bring or peel out, as a kernel from its enveloping husks its enveloping husks or shell. 2. (Med.) To remove without cutting (as a tumor). 3. To bring to light; to make clear. Sclater (1654).
enteric: Of or pertaining to the enteron, or alimentary canal; intestinal. Enteric fever (Med.), typhoid fever.
entasia: Tonic spasm; -- applied generically to denote any disease characterized by tonic spasms, as tetanus, trismus, etc.
environment: 1. Act of environing; state of being environed. 2. That which environs or surrounds; surrounding conditions, influences, or forces, by which living forms are influenced and modified in their growth and development. It is no friendly environment, this of thine. Carlyle.
enseam: To sew up; to inclose by a seam; hence, to include; to contain. Camden. | To cover with grease; to defile; to pollute. (old) In the rank sweat of an enseamed bed. Shak.

endoblastic: Relating to the endoblast; as, the endoblastic layer.
enrobe: To invest or adorn with a robe; to attire.
enneahedron: A figure having nine sides; a nonagon.
enwomb: 1. To conceive in the womb. (old) Spenser. 2. To bury, as it were in a womb; to hide, as in a gulf, pit, or cavern. Donne.
enchylemma: The basal substance of the cell nucleus; a hyaline or granular substance, more or less fluid during life, in which the other parts of the nucleus are imbedded.
enmanche: Resembling, or covered with, a sleeve; -- said of the chief when lines are drawn from the middle point of the upper edge upper edge to the sides.
encyclopedism: The art of writing or compiling encyclopedias; also, possession of the whole range of knowledge; encyclopedic learning.

ennuyee: A woman affected with ennui. Mrs. Jameson.

encyclopedical: Pertaining to, or of the nature of, an encyclopedia; embracing a wide range of subjects.
envier: One who envies; one who desires inordinately what another possesses.
enravish: To transport with delight; to enrapture; to fascinate. Spenser.

encage: To confine in a cage; to coop up. Shak.

endower: To endow. (old) Waterhouse. | One who endows.

endorhizous: Having the radicle of the embryo sheathed by the cotyledon, through which the embryo bursts in germination, as in many monocotyledonous plants.

endemiology: The science which treats of endemic affections.
entreative: Used in entreaty; pleading. "Entreative phrase." A. Brewer.

encomiastical: Bestowing praise; praising; eulogistic; laudatory; as, an encomiastic address or discourse. -- En*co`mi*as"tic*al*ly, adv.
encalendar: To register in a calendar; to calendar. Drayton.

endlessness: The quality of being endless; perpetuity.
enclitics: The art of declining and conjugating words.

entoglossal: Within the tongue; -- applied to the glossohyal bone.

enubilous: Free from fog, mist, or clouds; clear.
entoptic: Relating to objects situated within the eye; esp., relating to the perception of objects in one's own eye.
enthronization: The act of enthroning; hence, the admission of a bishop to his stall or throne in his cathedral.

englishism: 1. A quality or characteristic peculiar to the English. M. Arnold. 2. A form of expression peculiar to the English language as spoken in England; an Anglicism.

entasis: 1. (Arch.) A slight convex swelling of the shaft of a column. 2. (Med.) Same as Entasia.
environs: The parts or places which surround another place, or lie in its neighborhood; suburbs; as, the environs of a city or town. Chesterfield.
ensignship: The state or rank of an ensign.
entrick: To trick, to perplex. (old) Rom. of R.
entrap: To catch in a trap; to insnare; hence, to catch, as in a trap, by artifices; to involve in difficulties or distresses; to catch or involve in contradictions; as, to be entrapped by the devices of evil men. A golden mesh, to entrap the hearts of men. Shak. Syn. -- To insnare; inveigle; tangle; decoy; entangle.
enamelist: One who enamels; a workman or artist who applies enamels in ornamental work. [Written also enameller, enamellist.]
ensphere: 1. To place in a sphere; to envelop. His ample shoulders in a cloud ensphered. Chapman. 2. To form into a sphere.
encircle: To form a circle about; to inclose within a circle or ring; to surround; as, to encircle one in the arms; the army encircled the city. Her brows encircled with his serpent rod. Parnell. Syn. -- To encompass; surround; environ; inclose.
enshrine: To inclose in a shrine or chest; hence, to preserve or cherish as something sacred; as, to enshrine something in memory. We will enshrine it as holy relic. Massinger.
enneagynous: Having or producing nine pistils or styles; -- said of a flower or plant.
encapsulation: The act of inclosing in a capsule; the growth of a membrane around (any part) so as to inclose it in a capsule.
enlink: To chain together; to connect, as by links. Shak.
engineman: A man who manages, or waits on, an engine.
enhance: 1. To raise or lift up; to exalt. (old) Wyclif. Who, naught aghast, his mighty hand enhanced. Spenser. 2. To advance; to augment; to increase; to heighten; to make more costly or attractive; | To be raised up; to grow larger; as, a debt enhances rapidly by compound interest.
endurable: Capable of being endured or borne; sufferable. Macaulay. -- En*dur"a*ble*ness, n.
endostome: 1. (Bot.) The foramen or passage through the inner integument of an ovule. 2. (Zoöl.) And endostoma.
enduring: Lasting; durable; long-suffering; as, an enduring disposition. "A better and enduring substance." Heb. x. 34. -- En*dur"ing*ly, adv. T. Arnold. -- En*dur"ing*ness, n.
entrant: 1. One who enters; a beginner. "The entrant upon life." Bp. Terrot. 2. An applicant for admission. Stormonth.
enravishingly: So as to throw into ecstasy.
endogeny: Growth from within; multiplication of cells by endogenous division, as in the development of one or more cells in the interior of a parent cell.
endurance: 1. A state or quality of lasting or duration; lastingness; continuance. Slurring with an evasive answer the question concerning the endurance of his own possession. Sir W. Scott. 2. The act of bearing or suffering; a continuing under pain or distress without resistance, or without being overcome; sufferance; patience.
enneandria: A Linnæan class of plants having nine stamens.
envolume: To form into, or incorporate with, a volume.
endophragma: A chitinous structure above the nervous cord in the thorax of certain Crustacea.
enwrapment: Act of enwrapping; a wrapping or an envelope. Shuckford.
endermic: Acting through the skin, or by direct application to the skin. Endermic method, that in which the medicine enters the system through the skin, being applied either to the sound skin, or to the surface denuded of the cuticle by a blister.
ensample: An example; a pattern or model for imitation. (old) Tyndale. Being ensamples to the flock. | To exemplify, to show by example. (old) Spenser.
enschedule: To insert in a schedule. See Schedule. Shak.
enactment: 1. The passing of a bill into a law; the giving of legislative sanction and executive approval to a bill whereby it is established as a law. 2. That which is enacted or passed into a law; a law; a decree; a statute; a prescribed requirement; as, a prohibitory enactment; a social enactment.
enpatron: To act the part of a patron towards; to patronize. (old) Shak.
engrave: To deposit in the grave; to bury. (old) "Their corses to engrave." Spenser. | 1. To cut in; to make by incision. (old) Full many wounds in his corrupted flesh He did engrave. Spenser. 2. To cut with a graving instrument in order to form an inscription or pictorial…
enlivener: One who, or that which, enlivens, animates, or invigorates.
entice: To draw on, by exciting hope or desire; to allure; to attract; as, the bait enticed the fishes. Often in a bad sense: To lead astray; to induce to evil; to tempt; as, the sirens enticed them to listen. Roses blushing as they blow, And enticing men to pull. Beau. & Fl. My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not. Prov. i. 10.
enthusiastical: Filled with enthusiasm; characterized by enthusiasm; zealous; as, an enthusiastic lover of art. "Enthusiastical raptures." Calamy. -- En*thu`si*as"tic*al*ly, adv. A young man . . . of a visionary and enthusiastic character. W. Irving.
engaging: Tending to draw the attention or affections; attractive; as, engaging manners or address. -- En*ga"ging*ly, adv. -- En*ga"ging*ness, n. Engaging and disengaging gear or machinery, that in which, or by means of which, one part is alternately brought into gear or out of gear with another part, as occasion may require.
enouncement: Act of enouncing; that which is enounced.
endophloeum: The inner layer of the bark of trees.
encomiastic: Bestowing praise; praising; eulogistic; laudatory; as, an encomiastic address or discourse. -- En*co`mi*as"tic*al*ly, adv.
enterer: One who makes an entrance or beginning. A. Seward.
enthrallment: The act of enthralling, or state of being enthralled. See Inthrallment.
ensate: Having sword-shaped leaves, or appendages; ensiform.
enbloc: In a lump; as a whole; all together. "Movement of the ossicles en bloc." Nature. En bloc they are known as "the herd". W. A. Fraser.
engraving: 1. The act or art of producing upon hard material incised or raised patterns, characters, lines, and the like; especially, the art of producing such lines, etc., in the surface of metal plates or blocks of wood. Engraving is used for the decoration of the surface itself; also, for producing an original, from which a pattern or design may be printed on paper. 2.
enterotome: A kind of scissors used for opening the intestinal canal, as in post-mortem examinations.
enshield: To defend, as with a shield; to shield. (old) Shak. | Shielded; enshielded. (old) Shak.
enamor: To inflame with love; to charm; to captivate; -- with of, or with, before the person or thing; as, to be enamored with a lady; to be enamored of books or science. [Written also enamour.] Passionately enamored of this shadow of a dream. W. Irving.
endosperm: The albumen of a seed; -- limited by recent writers to that formed within the embryo sac.
endothelium: The thin epithelium lining the blood vessels, lymphatics, and serous cavities. See Epithelium.
enunciable: Capable of being enunciated or expressed.
enuresis: An involuntary discharge of urine; incontinence of urine.
entomb: To deposit in a tomb, as a dead body; to bury; to inter; to inhume. Hooker.
endeictic: Serving to show or exhibit; as, an endeictic dialogue, in the Platonic philosophy, is one which exhibits a specimen of skill. Enfield.
entirely: 1. In an entire manner; wholly; completely; fully; as, the trace is entirely lost. Euphrates falls not entirely into the Persian Sea. Raleigh. 2. Without alloy or mixture; truly; sincerely. To highest God entirely pray. Spenser.
engineer: 1. A person skilled in the principles and practice of any branch of engineering. See under Engineering, n. 2. One who manages as engine, particularly a steam engine; an engine driver. 3. | 1. To lay out or construct, as an engineer; to perform the work of an engineer on; as, to engineer a road. J. Hamilton. 2. To use contrivance and effort for; to guide the course of; to manage;
enomoty: A band of sworn soldiers; a division of the Spartan army ranging from twenty-five to thirty-six men, bound together by oath.
enigmatical: Relating to or resembling an enigma; not easily explained or accounted for; darkly expressed; obscure; puzzling; as, an enigmatical answer.
entry: 1. The act of entering or passing into or upon; entrance; ingress; hence, beginnings or first attempts; as, the entry of a person into a house or city; the entry of a river into the sea; the entry of air into the blood; an entry upon an undertaking. 2. The act of making or entering a record; a setting down in writing the particulars, as of a transaction;
enfoldment: The act of infolding. See Infoldment.
enlightener: One who enlightens or illuminates; one who, or that which, communicates light to the eye, or clear views to the mind.
envault: To inclose in a vault; to entomb. Swift.
endeavorer: One who makes an effort or attempt. [Written also endeavourer.]
energic: 1. In a state of action; acting; operating. 2. Having energy or great power; energetic. The energic faculty that we call will. Blackw. Mag.
enarthrosis: A ball and socket joint, or the kind of articulation represented by such a joint. See Articulation.
enteritis: An inflammation of the intestines. Hoblyn.
engagement: 1. The act of engaging, pledging, enlisting, occupying, or entering into contest. 2. The state of being engaged, pledged or occupied; specif., a pledge to take some one as husband or wife. 3. That which engages; engrossing occupation; employment of the attention; obligation by pledge, promise, or contract; an enterprise embarked in;
entangle: 1. To twist or interweave in such a manner as not to be easily separated; to make tangled, confused, and intricate; as, to entangle yarn or the hair. 2. To involve in such complications as to render extrication a bewildering difficulty; hence, metaphorically, to insnare; to perplex; to bewilder; to puzzle; as, to entangle the feet in a net, or in briers.
enjoy: 1. To take pleasure or satisfaction in the possession or experience of; to feel or perceive with pleasure; to be delighted with; as, to enjoy the dainties of a feast; to enjoy conversation. 2. | To take satisfaction; to live in happiness. Milton.
enharbor: To find harbor or safety in; to dwell in or inhabit. W. Browne.
endospore: The thin inner coat of certain spores.
energical: 1. In a state of action; acting; operating. 2. Having energy or great power; energetic. The energic faculty that we call will. Blackw. Mag.
entrammel: To trammel; to entangle. Bp. Hacket.
endecaphyllous: Composed of eleven leaflets; -- said of a leaf.
entozooelogist: One versed in the science of the Entozoa.
endanger: 1. To put to hazard; to bring into danger or peril; to expose to loss or injury; as, to endanger life or peace. All the other difficulties of his reign only exercised without endangering him. Burke. 2. To incur the hazard of; to risk. (old) He that turneth the humors back . . . endangereth malign ulcers. Bacon.
engore: 1. To gore; to pierce; to lacerate. (old) Deadly engored of a great wild boar. Spenser. 2. To make bloody. (old) Chapman.
encrinite: A fossil crinoid, esp. one belonging to, or resembling, the genus Encrinus. Sometimes used in a general sense for any crinoid.
enforcement: 1. The act of enforcing; compulsion. He that contendeth against these enforcements may easily master or resist them. Sir W. Raleigh. Confess 't was hers, and by what rough enforcement You got it from her. Shak. 2. A giving force to; a putting in execution. Enforcement of strict military discipline. Palfrey. 3.
encrimson: To give a crimson or red color to; to crimson. Shak.
enclitically: In an enclitic manner; by throwing the accent back. Walker.
entirety: 1. The state of being entire; completeness; as, entirely of interest. Blackstone. 2. That which is entire; the whole. Bacon.
entoil: To take with toils or bring into toils; to insnare. Entoiled in woofed phantasies. Keats.
enchafing: Heating; burning. (old) The wicked enchaufing or ardure of this sin [lust]. Chaucer.
entomotomy: The science of the dissection of insects.
enswathement: The act of enswathing, or the state of being enswathed.
entozoic: Pertaining to, or consisting of, the Entozoa.
engirdle: To surround as with a girdle; to girdle.
endosmosis: The transmission of a fluid or gas from without inward in the phenomena, or by the process, of osmose.
enation: Any unusual outgrowth from the surface of a thing, as of a petal; also, the capacity or act of producing such an outgrowth.
ennoble: 1. To make noble; to elevate in degree, qualities, or excellence; to dignify. "Ennobling all that he touches." Trench. What can ennoble sots, or slaves, or cowards Alas! not all the blood of all the Howards. Pope. 2. To raise to the rank of nobility; as, to ennoble a commoner. Syn. -- To raise; dignify; exalt; elevate; aggrandize.
encratite: One of a sect in the 2d century who abstained from marriage, wine, and animal food; -- called also Continent.
endochondral: Growing or developing within cartilage; -- applied esp. to developing bone.
enterocoele: A perivisceral cavity which arises as an outgrowth or outgrowths from the digestive tract; distinguished from a schizocoele, which arises by a splitting of the mesoblast of the embryo.
encompassment: The act of surrounding, or the state of being surrounded; circumvention. By this encompassment and drift of question. Shak.
enhunger: To make hungry. Those animal passions which vice had . . . enhungered to feed on innocence and life. J. Martineau.
engagedness: The state of being deeply interested; earnestness; zeal.
ennuye: Affected with ennui; weary in spirits; emotionally exhausted. | One who is affected with ennui.
endospermic: Relating to, accompanied by, or containing, endosperm.
enterocele: A hernial tumor whose contents are intestine.
entrain: To draw along as a current does; as, water entrained by steam. | To put aboard a railway train; as, to entrain a regiment. [Recent, Eng.]
enthronement: The act of enthroning, or state of being enthroned. [Recent]
entermewer: A hawk gradually changing the color of its feathers, commonly in the second year.
enfeloned: Rendered fierce or frantic. (old) "Like one enfeloned or distraught." Spenser.
entomology: 1. That part of zoölogy which treats of insects. 2. A treatise on the science of entomology.
entwine: To twine, twist, or wreathe together or round. [Written also intwine.] Entwined in duskier wreaths her braided locks. Shelley. Thy glorious household stuff did me entwine. Herbert. | To be twisted or twined. With whose imperial laurels might entwine no cypress. De Quincey.
enable: 1. To give strength or ability to; to make firm and strong. (old) "Who hath enabled me." 1 Tim. i. 12. Receive the Holy Ghost, said Christ to his apostles, when he enabled them with priestly power. Jer. Taylor. 2. To make able (to do, or to be, something); to confer sufficient power upon; to furnish with means, opportunities, and the like; to render competent for; to empower;
encoach: To carry in a coach. Davies (Wit's Pilgr.)
entryng: Am entrance. (old) So great an entryng and so large. Chaucer.
enseel: To close eyes of; to seel; -- said in reference to a hawk. (old)
enisled: Placed alone or apart, as if on an island; severed, as an island. "In the sea of life enisled." M. Arnold.
engrail: 1. To variegate or spot, as with hail. A caldron new engrailed with twenty hues. Chapman. 2. (Her.) To indent with small curves. See Engrailed. | To form an edging or border; to run in curved or indented lines. Parnell.
encrinic: Relating to encrinites; containing encrinites, as certain kinds of limestone.
enface: 1. To write or print on the face of (a draft, bill, etc.); as, to enface drafts with memoranda. 2. To write or print (a memorandum, direction, or the like) on the face of a draft, bill, etc.; as, to enface the words "Payable in Calcutta" upon the face of a draft.
encounterer: One who encounters; an opponent; an antagonist. Atterbury.
ensemble: The whole; all the parts taken together.
envoyship: The office or position of an envoy.
engle: A favorite; a paramour; an ingle. (old) B. Jonson. | To cajole or coax, as favorite. (old) I 'll presently go and engle some broker. B. Jonson.
envolup: To wrap up; to envelop. (old) Chaucer.
entozoal: Pertaining to, or consisting of, the Entozoa.
engaged: 1. Occupied; employed; busy. 2. Pledged; promised; especially, having the affections pledged; promised in marriage; affianced; betrothed. 3. Greatly interested; of awakened zeal; earnest. 4. Involved; esp., involved in a hostile encounter; as, the engaged ships continued the fight. Engaged column. (Arch.) Same as Attached column. See under Attach, v. t.
encarpus: An ornament on a frieze or capital, consisting of festoons of fruit, flowers, leaves, etc. [Written also encarpa.]
endurant: Capable of enduring fatigue, pain, hunger, etc. The ibex is a remarkably endurant animal. J. G. Wood.
endmost: Farthest; remotest; at the very end. Tylor.
enchanting: Having a power of enchantment; charming; fascinating. -- En*chant"ing*ly, adv.
endotheca: The tissue which partially fills the interior of the interseptal chambers of most madreporarian corals. It usually consists of a series of oblique tranverse septa, one above another. -- En`do*the"cal, a.
engarrison: To garrison; to put in garrison, or to protect by a garrison. Bp. Hall.
enavigate: To sail away or over. (old) Cockeram.
enterpriser: One who undertakes enterprises. Sir J. Hayward.
enthymematical: Pertaining to, or of the form of, an enthymeme.
engorge: 1. To gorge; to glut. Mir. for Mag. 2. To swallow with greediness or in large quantities; to devour. Spenser. | To feed with eagerness or voracity; to stuff one's self with food. Beaumont.
entrochal: Pertaining to, or consisting of, entrochites, or the joints of encrinites; -- used of a kind of stone or marble.
enrapture: To transport with pleasure; to delight beyond measure; to enravish. Shenstone.
engineering: Originally, the art of managing engines; in its modern and extended sense, the art and science by which the mechanical properties of matter are made useful to man in structures and machines; the occupation and work of an engineer. Note: In a comprehensive sense, engineering includes architecture as a mechanical art, in distinction from architecture as a fine art.
enmity: 1. The quality of being an enemy; hostile or unfriendly disposition. No ground of enmity between us known. Milton. 2. A state of opposition; hostility. The friendship of the world is enmity with God. James iv. 4. Syn. -- Rancor; hostility; hatred; aversion; antipathy; repugnance; animosity; ill will; malice; malevolence. See Animosity, Rancor.
enslavement: The act of reducing to slavery; state of being enslaved; bondage; servitude. A fresh enslavement to their enemies. South.
enfeeblement: The act of weakening; enervation; weakness.
enfiled: Having some object, as the head of a man or beast, impaled upon it; as, a sword which is said to be "enfiled of" the thing which it pierces.
enact: 1. To decree; to establish by legal and authoritative act; to make into a law; especially, to perform the legislative act with reference to (a bill) which gives it the validity of law. 2. To act; to perform; to do; to effect. (old) The king enacts more wonders than a man. Shak. 3. To act the part of; to represent; to play. I did enact Julius Caesar. Shak.
endaspidean: Having the anterior scutes extending around the tarsus on the inner side; -- said of certain birds.
encaustic: Prepared by means of heat; burned in. Encaustic painting (Fine Arts), painting by means of wax with which the colors are combined, and which is afterwards fused with hot irons, thus fixing the… | The method of painting in heated wax, or in any way where heat is used to fix the colors.
endome: To cover as with a dome.
encave: To hide in, or as in, a cave or recess. "Do but encave yourself." Shak.
enantiopathy: 1. An opposite passion or affection. Sir W. Hamilton. 2. (Med.) Allopathy; -- a term used by followers of Hahnemann, or homeopathists.
engraved: 1. Made by engraving or ornamented with engraving. 2. (Zoöl.) Having the surface covered with irregular, impressed lines.
endothorax: An internal process of the sternal plates in the thorax of insects.
entelechy: An actuality; a conception completely actualized, in distinction from mere potential existence.
enteropneusta: A group of wormlike invertebrates having, along the sides of the body, branchial openings for the branchial sacs, which are formed by diverticula of the alimentary canal. Balanoglossus is the only known genus. See Illustration in Appendix.
enlimn: To adorn by illuminating or ornamenting with colored and decorated letters and figures, as a book or manuscript. Palsgrave.
engallant: To make a gallant of. (old) B. Jonson.
endophragmal: Of or pertaining to the endophragma.
endowment: 1. The act of bestowing a dower, fund, or permanent provision for support. 2. That which is bestowed or settled on a person or an institution; property, fund, or revenue permanently appropriated to any object; as, the endowment of a church, a hospital, or a college. 3. That which is given or bestowed upon the person or mind; gift of nature; accomplishment; natural capacity;
encyclopedia: The circle of arts and sciences; a comprehensive summary of knowledge, or of a branch of knowledge; esp., a work in which the various branches of science or art are discussed separately, and usually in alphabetical order; a cyclopedia.
enchantress: A woman versed in magical arts; a sorceress; also, a woman who fascinates. Shak.
endopleurite: The portion of each apodeme developed from the interepimeral membrane in certain crustaceans.
enhydros: A variety of chalcedony containing water.
entozooen: One of the Entozoa. ENTR'ACTE En`tr'acte", n. Etym: [F. Cf. Interact.] 1. The interval of time which occurs between the performance of any two acts of a drama. 2. A dance, piece of music, or interlude, performed between two acts of a drama.
encyclopedic: Pertaining to, or of the nature of, an encyclopedia; embracing a wide range of subjects.
entombment: The act of entombing or burying, or state of being entombed; burial. Barrow.
endurer: One who, or that which, endures or lasts; one who bears, suffers, or sustains.
enchest: To inclose in a chest. Vicars.
enharmonically: In the enharmonic style or system; in just intonation.
envyned: Stored or furnished with wine. (old) Chaucer.
entertaining: Affording entertainment; pleasing; amusing; diverting. -- En`ter*tain"ing*ly, adv. -- En`ter*tain"ing*ness, n.
enflower: To cover or deck with flowers. (poetic) These odorous and enflowered fields. B. Jonson.
enascent: Coming into being; nascent. (old) Bp. Warburton.
enlute: To coat with clay; to lute. (old) Chaucer.
enantiosis: A figure of speech by which what is to be understood affirmatively is stated negatively, and the contrary; affirmation by contraries.
endodermic: Of or pertaining to the endoderm.
encomiast: One who praises; a panegyrist. Locke.
englut: 1. To swallow or gulp down. (old) Shak. 2. To glut. (old) "Englutted with vanity." Ascham.
endothermic: Designating, or pert. to, a reaction which occurs with absorption of heat; formed by such a reaction; as, an endothermic substance; -- opposed to exothermic.
enodation: The act or operation of clearing of knots, or of untying; hence, also, the solution of a difficulty. Bailey.
enaliosauria: An extinct group of marine reptiles, embracing both the Ichthyosauria and the Plesiosauria, now regarded as distinct orders.
entophyte: A vegetable parasite subsisting in the interior of the body.
entanglement: State of being entangled; intricate and confused involution; that which entangles; intricacy; perplexity.
endoplastica: A group of Rhizopoda having a distinct nucleus, as the am
endecagon: A plane figure of eleven sides and angles.
endlong: Lengthwise; along. (old) The doors were all of adamants eterne, I-clenched overthwart and endelong With iron tough. Chaucer. He pricketh endelong the large space. Chaucer. To thrust the raft endlong across the moat. Sir W. Scott.
enigmatic: Relating to or resembling an enigma; not easily explained or accounted for; darkly expressed; obscure; puzzling; as, an enigmatical answer.
engrosser: 1. One who copies a writing in large, fair characters. 2. One who takes the whole; a person who purchases such quantities of articles in a market as to raise the price; a forestaller. Locke.
encolure: The neck of horse. R. Browning.
enhort: To encourage. (old) "To enhort the people." Chaucer.
encenia: A festival commemorative of the founding of a city or the consecration of a church; also, the ceremonies (as at Oxford and Cambridge, England) commemorative of founders or benefactors.
enfroward: To make froward, perverse, or ungovernable. (old) Sir E. Sandys.
enablement: The act of enabling, or the state of being enabled; ability. Bacon.
entertain: 1. To be at the charges of; to take or keep in one's service; to maintain; to support; to harbor; to keep. You, sir, I entertain for one of my hundred. Shak. 2. To give hospitable reception and… | To receive, or provide entertainment for, guests; as, he entertains generously.
entree: 1. A coming in, or entrance; hence, freedom of access; permission or right to enter; as, to have the entrée of a house. 2. (Cookery) In French usage, a dish served at the beginning of dinner to give zest to the appetite; in English usage, a side dish, served with a joint, or between the courses, as a cutlet, scalloped oysters, etc.
enactive: Having power to enact or establish as a law. Abp. Bramhall.
enormity: 1. The state or quality of exceeding a measure or rule, or of being immoderate, monstrous, or outrageous. The enormity of his learned acquisitions. De Quincey. 2. That which is enormous; especially, an exceeding offense against order, right, or decency; an atrocious crime; flagitious villainy; an atrocity.
englishman: A native or a naturalized inhabitant of England.
encephaloid: Resembling the material of the brain; cerebriform. Encephaloid cancer (Med.), a very malignant form of cancer of brainlike consistency. See under Cancer.
ensoul: To indue or imbue (a body) with soul. Emerson.
enniche: To place in a niche. Sterne.
engouled: Partly swallowed; disappearing in the jaws of anything; as, an infant engouled by a serpent; said also of an ordinary, when its two ends to issue from the mouths of lions, or the like; as, a bend engouled.
endoskeletal: Pertaining to, or connected with, the endoskeleton; as, endoskeletal muscles.
entomere: The more granular cells, which finally become internal, in many segmenting ova, as those of mammals.
engaol: To put in jail; to imprison. (old) Shak.
entoplasm: (a) The inner granular layer of protoplasm in a developing ovum. (b) Endosarc.
endosporous: Having the spores contained in a case; -- applied to fungi.
enshroud: To cover with, or as with, a shroud; to shroud. Churchill.
endamage: To bring loss or damage to; to harm; to injure. The trial hath endamaged thee no way. Milton.
engarboil: To throw into disorder; to disturb. (old) "To engarboil the church." Bp. Montagu.
encourager: One who encourages, incites, or helps forward; a favorer. The pope is . . . a great encourager of arts. Addison.
enchair: To seat in a chair. Tennyson.
enumerate: To count; to tell by numbers; to count over, or tell off one after another; to number; to reckon up; to mention one by one; to name over; to make a special and separate account of; to recount; as, to enumerate the stars in a constellation. Enumerating the services he had done. Ludlow. Syn. -- To reckon; compute; calculate; count; estimate; relate; rehearse; recapitulate;
endosmose: The transmission of a fluid or gas from without inward in the phenomena, or by the process, of osmose.
endoneurium: The delicate bands of connective tissue among nerve fibers.
envermeil: To color with, or as with, vermilion; to dye red. (old) Milton.
encyclopedian: Embracing the whole circle of learning, or a wide range of subjects.
energetical: 1. Having energy or energies; possessing a capacity for vigorous action or for exerting force; active. "A Being eternally energetic." Grew. 2. Exhibiting energy; operating with force, vigor, and effect; forcible; powerful; efficacious; as, energetic measures; energetic laws. Syn. -- Forcible; powerful; efficacious; potent; vigorous; effective; strenuous.
enervation: 1. The act of weakening, or reducing strength. 2. The state of being weakened; effeminacy. Bacon.
encyclopedist: The compiler of an encyclopedia, or one who assists in such compilation; also, one whose knowledge embraces the whole range of the sciences. The Encyclopedists, the writers of the great French encyclopedia which appeared in 1751-1772. The editors were Diderot and D'Alembert. Among the contributors were Voltaire and Rousseau.
enrockment: A mass of large stones thrown into water at random to form bases of piers, breakwaters, etc.
enameled: Coated or adorned with enamel; having a glossy or variegated surface; glazed. [Written also enamelled.]
entoprocta: A group of Bryozoa in which the anus is within the circle of tentacles. See Pedicellina.
enchase: 1. To incase or inclose in a border or rim; to surround with an ornamental casing, as a gem with gold; to encircle; to inclose; to adorn. Enchased with a wanton ivy twine. Spenser. An precious stones, in studs of gold enchased, The shaggy velvet of his buskins graced. Mickle. 2. To chase; to ornament by embossing or engraving; as, to enchase a watch case. With golden letters .
encrinital: Relating to encrinites; containing encrinites, as certain kinds of limestone.
endochrome: The coloring matter within the cells of plants, whether green, red, yellow, or any other color.
endoparasite: Any parasite which lives in the internal organs of an animal, as the tapeworms, Trichina, etc.; -- opposed to ectoparasite. See Entozoön. -- En`do*par`a*sit"ic, a.
ensnare: To catch in a snare. See Insnare.
energizing: Capable of imparting or exercising energy. Those nobler exercises of energizing love. Bp. Horsley.
enswathe: To swathe; to envelop, as in swaddling clothes. Shak.
enorthotrope: An optical toy; a card on which confused or imperfect figures are drawn, but which form to the eye regular figures when the card is rapidly revolved. See Thaumatrope.
entail: 1. That which is entailed. Hence: (Law) (a) An estate in fee entailed, or limited in descent to a particular class of issue. (b) The rule by which the descent is fixed. | 1. To settle or fix inalienably on a person or thing, or on a person and his descendants or a certain line of descendants; -- said especially of an estate; to bestow as an heritage.
enervate: To deprive of nerve, force, strength, or courage; to render feeble or impotent; to make effeminate; to impair the moral powers of. A man . . . enervated by licentiousness. Macaulay. | Weakened; weak; without strength of force. Pope.
enlighten: 1. To supply with light; to illuminate; as, the sun enlightens the earth. His lightnings enlightened the world. Ps. xcvii. 4. 2. To make clear to the intellect or conscience; to shed the light of truth and knowledge upon; to furnish with increase of knowledge; to instruct; as, to enlighten the mind or understanding. The conscience enlightened by the Word and Spirit of God.
endosteal: Relating to endostosis; as, endosteal ossification.
enlargement: 1. The act of increasing in size or bulk, real or apparent; the state of being increased; augmentation; further extension; expansion. 2. Expansion or extension, as of the powers of the mind; ennoblement, as of the feelings and character; as, an enlargement of views, of knowledge, of affection. 3. A setting at large, or being set at large;
enviable: Fitted to excite envy; capable of awakening an ardent desire to posses or to resemble. One of most enviable of human beings. Macaulay. -- En"vi*a*ble*ness, n. -- En"vi*a*bly, adv.
enfetter: To bind in fetters; to enchain. "Enfettered to her love." Shak.
enseal: To impress with a seal; to mark as with a seal; hence, to ratify. (old) This deed I do enseal. Piers Plowman.
enginesized: Sized by a machine, and not while in the pulp; -- said of paper. Knight.
enomotarch: The commander of an enomoty. Mitford.
endocardiac: 1. Pertaining to the endocardium. 2. (Med.) Seated or generated within the heart; as, endocardial murmurs.
enjoin: 1. To lay upon, as an order or command; to give an injunction to; to direct with authority; to order; to charge. High matter thou enjoin'st me. Milton. I am enjoined by oath to observe three things. | To join or unite. (old) Hooker.
ensiform: Having the form of a sword blade; sword-shaped; as, an ensiform leaf. Ensiform cartilage, and Ensiform process. (Anat.) See Xiphisternum.
entrancement: The act of entrancing, or the state of trance or ecstasy. Otway.
ensear: To sear; to dry up. (old) Ensear thy fertile and conceptious womb. Shak.
encashment: The payment in cash of a note, draft, etc.
entoplastic: Pertaining to, or composed of, entoplasm; as, the entoplastic products of some Protozoa, or the entoplastic modification of the cell protoplasm, by which a nucleus is produced.
endways: 1. On end; erectly; in an upright position. 2. With the end forward.
encrinus: A genus of fossil encrinoidea, from the Mesozoic rocks.
enarched: Bent into a curve; -- said of a bend or other ordinary.
engorgement: 1. The act of swallowing greedily; a devouring with voracity; a glutting. 2. (Med.) An overfullness or obstruction of the vessels in some part of the system; congestion. Hoblyn. 3. (Metal.) The clogging of a blast furnace.
entoperipheral: Being, or having its origin, within the external surface of the body; -- especially applied to feelings, such as hunger, produced by internal disturbances. Opposed to epiperipheral.
enaliosaurian: Pertaining to the Enaliosauria. -- n. One of the Enaliosauria.
entomological: Of or relating to entomology. -- En`to*mo*log"ic*al*ly, adv.
enemy: One hostile to another; one who hates, and desires or attempts the injury of, another; a foe; an adversary; as, an enemy of or to a person; an enemy to truth, or to falsehood. | Hostile; inimical. (old) They . . . every day grow more enemy to God. Jer. Taylor.
encense: To offer incense to or upon; to burn incense. (old) Chaucer.
entoplastron: The median plate of the plastron of turtles; -- called also entosternum.
ensign: 1. A flag; a banner; a standard; esp., the national flag, or a banner indicating nationality, carried by a ship or a body of soldiers; -- as distinguished from flags indicating divisions of the army,… | 1. To designate as by an ensign. (old) Henry but joined the roses that ensigned Particular families. B. Jonson. 2. To distinguish by a mark or ornament; esp. (Her.), by a crown;
enucleation: The act of enucleating; elucidation; exposition. Neither sir, nor water, nor food, seem directly to contribute anything to the enucleation of this disease. Tooke.
endeavor: To exert physical or intellectual strength for the attainment of; to use efforts to effect; to strive to achieve or reach; to try; to attempt. It is our duty to endeavor the recovery of these… | To exert one's self; to work for a certain end. And such were praised who but endeavored well. Pope. Note: Usually with an infinitive; as, to endeavor to outstrip an antagonist. He had . . .
endoscopy: The art or process of examining by means of the endoscope.
endiaper: To decorate with a diaper pattern.
enchainment: The act of enchaining, or state of being enchained.
enfouldred: Mixed with, or emitting, lightning. (old) "With foul enfouldred smoke." Spenser.
enhedge: To surround as with a hedge. Vicars.
enkerchiefed: Bound with a kerchief; draped; hooded; covered. Milton. That soft, enkerchiefed hair. M. Arnold.
encroacher: One who by gradual steps enters on, and takes possession of, what is not his own.
enunciatory: Pertaining to, or containing, enunciation or utterance.
enthusiastic: Filled with enthusiasm; characterized by enthusiasm; zealous; as, an enthusiastic lover of art. "Enthusiastical raptures." Calamy. -- En*thu`si*as"tic*al*ly, adv. A young man . . . | An enthusiast; a zealot. (old)
enumeration: 1. The act of enumerating, making separate mention, or recounting. 2. A detailed account, in which each thing is specially noticed. Because almost every man we meet possesses these, we leave them out of our enumeration. Paley. 3. (Rhet.) A recapitulation, in the peroration, of the heads of an argument.
endogen: A plant which increases in size by internal growth and elongation at the summit, having the wood in the form of bundles or threads, irregularly distributed throughout the whole diameter, not forming annual layers, and with no distinct pith.
entailment: 1. The act of entailing or of giving, as an estate, and directing the mode of descent. 2. The condition of being entailed. 3. A thing entailed. Brutality as an hereditary entailment becomes an ever weakening force. R. L. Dugdale.
enthrall: To hold in thrall; to enslave. See Inthrall. The bars survive the captive they enthrall. Byron.
enmist: To infold, as in a mist.
enfeebler: One who, or that which, weakens or makes feeble.
endothecium: The inner lining of an another cell.
enzooetic: Afflicting animals; -- used of a disease affecting the animals of a district. It corresponds to an endemic disease among men.
entheal: Divinely inspired; wrought up to enthusiasm. (old)
enrich: 1. To make rich with any kind of wealth; to render opulent; to increase the possessions of; as, to enrich the understanding with knowledge. Seeing, Lord, your great mercy Us hath enriched so openly. Chaucer's Dream. 2. To supply with ornament; to adorn; as, to enrich a ceiling by frescoes. 3. To make rich with manure; to fertilize; -- said of the soil;
encysted: Inclosed in a cyst, or a sac, bladder, or vesicle; as, an encysted tumor. The encysted venom, or poison bag, beneath the adder's fang. Coleridge.
enginer: A contriver; an inventor; a contriver of engines. (old) Shak.
endemic: Peculiar to a district or particular locality, or class of persons; as, an endemic disease. Note: An endemic disease is one which is constantly present to a greater or less degree in any place, as… | An endemic disease. Fear, which is an endemic latent in every human heart, sometimes rises into an epidemic. J. B. Heard.
endoskeleton: The bony, cartilaginous, or other internal framework of an animal, as distinguished from the exoskeleton.
entastic: Relating to any disease characterized by tonic spasms.
enchanted: Under the power of enchantment; possessed or exercised by enchanters; as, an enchanted castle.
entertainment: 1. The act of receiving as host, or of amusing, admitting, or cherishing; hospitable reception; also, reception or treatment, in general. The entertainment of Christ by faith. Baxter. The sincere entertainment and practice of the precepts of the gospel. Bp. Sprat. 2. That which entertains, or with which one is entertained; as: (a) Hospitality;
enneagonal: Belonging to an enneagon; having nine angles.
enamelar: Consisting of enamel; resembling enamel; smooth; glossy. Craig.
enterprise: 1. That which is undertaken; something attempted to be performed; a work projected which involves activity, courage, energy, and the like; a bold, arduous, or hazardous attempt; an undertaking; | 1. To undertake; to begin and attempt to perform; to venture upon. The business must be enterprised this night. Dryden. What would I not renounce or enterprise for you! T. Otway. 2.
endocyst: The inner layer of the cells of Bryozoa.
entend: To attend to; to apply one's self to. (old) Chaucer.
entobronchium: One of the main bronchi in the lungs of birds.
ensconce: To cover or shelter, as with a sconce or fort; to place or hide securely; to conceal. She shall not see me: I will ensconce me behind the arras. Shak.
enameler: One who enamels; a workman or artist who applies enamels in ornamental work. [Written also enameller, enamellist.]
enliven: 1. To give life, action, or motion to; to make vigorous or active; to excite; to quicken; as, fresh fuel enlivens a fire. Lo! of themselves th' enlivened chessmen move. Cowley. 2. To give spirit or vivacity to; to make sprightly, gay, or cheerful; to animate; as, mirth and good humor enliven a company; enlivening strains of music. Syn. -- To animate; rouse; inspire; cheer;
enrollment: 1. The act of enrolling; registration. Holland. 2. A writing in which anything is enrolled; a register; a record. Sir J. Davies.
enubilate: To clear from mist, clouds, or obscurity. Bailey.
endomorph: A crystal of one species inclosed within one of another, as one of rutile inclosed in quartz.
